packets.title: One ballot, 120 seats
packets.audience: Readers new to Israeli elections; pairs or a small discussion group.
packets.prerequisites: No prior knowledge. A browser is useful for the linked guides but not required for the exercise.
objectives: Explain the 3.25% threshold and what happens below it.
Distinguish an electoral list from a bloc.
Explain why the largest list does not automatically form a government.

learner.heading: Read together (3 minutes)
paragraphs: Voters choose a ranked electoral list in a single nationwide constituency. There are 120 Knesset seats. An electoral list can contain more than one party; a bloc is a grouping of lists used to describe possible cooperation.
A list must receive at least 3.25% of valid votes to win seats. Votes for a list below the threshold are not transferred to another list. Seats are allocated among the lists that pass.

The largest list does not automatically form the government. Government formation involves a presidential mandate, a proposed governing arrangement and Knesset confidence. An absolute seat majority is 61 of 120; that planning target alone does not establish the legal outcome of a confidence vote.

learner.heading: A fictional ballot (5 minutes)
paragraphs: Assume every vote is valid: List A receives 40%, B receives 30%, C receives 27% and D receives 3%. These are invented lists, not Israeli parties.
prompts: Which lists pass the threshold? What happens to D's votes?
The passing vote shares sum to what percentage? Why should a seat calculation use that passing pool rather than transferring D's votes?
A is the largest list. What else would you need to know before saying A will govern?

learner.heading: Explain it to a partner (4 minutes)
prompts: Finish: A party/list differs from a bloc because…
Finish: 61 describes… It does not prove…
Name one distinction between national voting eligibility and being affected by a government's decisions. Consult Who votes if you are unsure.

learner.heading: Leave with one question (3 minutes)
prompts: What would you inspect next: a party's evidence, a coalition's partners or a poll's method? Explain your choice.

facilitator.heading: Set up and pace
paragraphs: Give learners the sheet. Read the opening aloud, work in pairs on the fictional ballot, then invite explanations rather than a show of hands. Allow 3 minutes to read, 5 for the ballot, 4 for partner explanations and 3 for a closing question.
Keep the three objectives visible. Let participants skip a question. A phone is enough to open the guides; the printed sheet supplies the core facts.

facilitator.heading: Answer notes
paragraphs: A, B and C pass; D does not. D receives no seats, and its votes are not transferred to an ally. Passing lists account for 97% of the valid vote. Their relative shares form the seat-allocation pool; exact whole-seat allocation also uses the Bader-Ofer rules.

Being largest does not identify which lists will cooperate, the proposed prime minister, confidence support or policy conditions. The builder's seat target and recorded commitments are separate evidence.

An electoral list is a ballot choice and may include constituent parties. A bloc is a grouping for analysis. A 61-seat grouping has an absolute majority; do not turn this into a universal statement about every confidence vote.

National eligibility depends on citizenship and legal conditions. Residents and people affected by decisions are not one legal category. The Who votes guide distinguishes Palestinian citizens, East Jerusalem permanent residents and Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and Gaza.

facilitator.heading: Questions worth pursuing
paragraphs: Ask: What would make an apparently simple arithmetic answer misleading? Which facts are legal rules, which are current political commitments, and which are our hypothetical assumptions?

If participants ask for today's numbers, open the polls rather than reading an old number from a slide. Record the publication date and the average's method before comparing it with an individual poll.

facilitator.heading: Check understanding and adapt
paragraphs: Before finishing, ask two people to explain the threshold, list/bloc distinction and largest-list point in their own words. Correct misconceptions with the guide evidence rather than partisan examples.

For a 30-minute session, add the five-minute guided route and compare two party profiles. For remote teaching, share the accessible HTML sheet and invite spoken or typed responses. Treat unfamiliar-reader feedback as evidence for improving the lesson.

packets.title: Enough seats; what cooperation?
packets.audience: A discussion group familiar with the threshold and 120-seat Knesset.
packets.prerequisites: Read the system learner sheet or complete the five-minute guided route. Use the builder for the optional real-world follow-up.
objectives: Separate an absolute seat majority from confidence support and governing cooperation.
Distinguish a shared objective, a policy conflict and missing evidence.

learner.heading: Your fictional Knesset (5 minutes)
paragraphs: Six invented lists hold 120 seats: A 46, B 17, C 11, D 9, E 7 and F 30. These are a teaching exercise, not actual parties, polls or a forecast.

A favors a common school curriculum. B favors autonomy for faith schools. C favors a common curriculum too, while D has no recorded answer. Those statements are invented assumptions for this exercise.
prompts: Choose two different groups of lists that reach the 61-seat absolute-majority target. Write each total.
For each group, remove one partner at a time. Which partners are indispensable for keeping 61 seats?

learner.heading: From a total to an arrangement (10 minutes)
prompts: Compare A+B with A+C+D. Identify the policy difference in one arrangement and the missing evidence in the other.
What would you ask B or D before describing a workable shared school policy? Draft one possible compromise; mark it hypothetical.
Distinguish cabinet membership, outside confidence support, opposition and abstention. What must be verified before deciding how a particular confidence vote would work?
What leadership or implementation question remains even if everyone agrees on an objective?

learner.heading: Test the real tools (10 minutes, optional)
paragraphs: Open one existing classroom scenario and the linked builder. Keep its date and recorded commitments visible. Open Compare for the same selection.
prompts: Record the selected poll or average and publication date. Does changing the poll change the absolute-majority conclusion?
Find one shared recorded answer, one difference and one missing answer. Read the original evidence before calling anything a red line.
Name two obstacles or compromises that arithmetic alone cannot resolve. Separate what a party actually said from your own proposal.

learner.heading: Exit reflection (5 minutes)
prompts: Explain: enough seats is a starting point because…
What new evidence would change your account of this arrangement?

facilitator.heading: Preparation and timing
paragraphs: Begin with the fictional Knesset so the group can practice distinctions before arguing over actual parties. All hypothetical seat and policy assumptions are on the learner sheet. Allow 5 minutes for arithmetic, 10 for arrangements, 10 for the tools and 5 for reflection.
If the group has no devices, extend the fictional policy discussion and omit the optional tool exercise. Printed sources and answer notes keep the lesson usable offline.

facilitator.heading: Arithmetic answer notes
paragraphs: A+B has 63 seats. Removing B leaves 46, and removing A leaves 17; both are needed for this group's absolute majority. A+C+D has 66; removing C leaves 55 and removing D leaves 57, so both smaller partners are indispensable too.
Many other combinations reach 61, including A+F with 76. Mathematical feasibility alone says nothing about a recorded willingness to cooperate. Do not imply invented lists represent actual parties.

facilitator.heading: Evidence and compromise answer notes
paragraphs: A and B disagree on a school-policy mechanism; ask what autonomy or common curriculum means before declaring it irreconcilable. A and C share a recorded objective, but D's missing answer cannot establish coalition-wide agreement.
A proposed common core plus autonomy in other subjects is a hypothetical compromise, not a reported promise. Even shared goals leave funding, implementation, leadership and enforcement questions.

Outside support and abstention differ from cabinet membership. Verify the current confidence rules and declared commitments; do not equate a 61-seat planning target with every legal confidence vote. The linked formation guide supplies the legal evidence.

facilitator.heading: Facilitate the real-world extension
paragraphs: Choose any existing teaching scenario, including a Netanyahu-led one. Apply the same questions to every grouping. Ask learners to record the poll and evidence date instead of memorizing a total.

A missing position is an evidence limit, and a category match is not a stability score. Ask what is observed, what is inferred, what is hypothetical and what remains unknown. Invite disagreement about interpretations while keeping factual claims source-based.

Conclude by asking learners to name two concrete obstacles or compromises. If they offer only a seat total, return to leadership, confidence, recorded commitments and the policy evidence. Do not grade participants for choosing a political camp.
